description: β numerical validation — Monte Carlo check of the analytical variance formula for the octonion associator, Fano-triple case. Setup (per docs/research/variance_of_associator.md § "Worked example:
comments: β numerical validation — Monte Carlo check of the analytical variance
formula for the octonion associator, Fano-triple case.
Setup (per docs/research/variance_of_associator.md § "Worked example:
single Fano generator"):
A(a, b, c) := ‖[a, b, c]‖²   where [a,b,c] = (a·b)·c − a·(b·c)
Unperturbed: [a,b,c] = 2·e_7, A = 4.
Perturb a_1 → 1 + δ, δ ~ N(0, σ²). The analytical first-order GUM
variance (from the β document, derivation):
Var(A) ≈ 64 σ²                                (TRUTH)
If the current compiler's stepwise scalar-product rule were applied
instead, it would give:
Var_compiler(A) ≈ 16 σ²                       (COMPILER, 4× low)
This test computes the sample variance of A over N = 100,000 Monte
Carlo samples and compares to the TRUTH formula. It does NOT test the
compiler's variance_of() — that requires the full Knowledge<f64>
chain which introduces unrelated complexities (see ζ buffer bug). The
compiler comparison is deferred to a separate test.
Pass criterion: |MC_var − 64σ²| / 64σ² < 0.05 (5% relative error).
If this passes, β's analytical formula is validated empirically. The
remaining claim — that the compiler produces 16σ² — is then a
separate reading-confirmation task.

Returning a nested array literal from a function declared to return a 2-D
array is rejected: `error: return type does not match function signature`.
The flat case is accepted, so the gap is specific to the nested encoding. The
declared type comes from scan_type and the literal builds its own hash from

discriminator -- [[f64; 1]; 2], whose inner element is 8 bytes, is rejected
too, so a first guess that scan_type computes a real element size while the
literal hardcodes 8 is disproven.
This matters beyond arrays. The return-type check currently reports through
tc_error, which prints "warning: " and does not fail the build (see the note
at its definition). Pointing it at tc_error_hard makes it fatal and works --
it correctly rejects hello.sio and bdf_stiff.sio, which really are ill-typed
-- but it also rejects this, and stdlib/numerical/linalg.sio mat7_to_nested,
which are correct. So the return position cannot be made to fail a build
until this is fixed, and that is the whole dependency: nothing else in the
study's 24 modules or in 1893 run-pass tests is affected.

A basis-aligned octonion candidate is a 3-dim F₂ subspace of the sedenion index space F₂⁴ (its 7
nonzero vectors, XOR-closed); there are 15. This test certifies three exact partitions of them:
* NSUB = 15 subspaces total;
* ZDFREE = 8 are zero-divisor-free (genuine octonion / division algebra); the other 7 contain a
zero divisor — the quasi-octonions (matches Cawagas, Discuss. Math. 2004: 7 quasi-octonions carry
the sedenion zero divisors);
* PURE = 1 is "Clifford-pure" — has ALL C(7,2)=21 internal ambient left-mult pairs anticommuting
({L_i,L_j}=0 in the 16-dim Cℓ(8), see sedenion_clifford8.md): the base octonion {e_1..e_7}.
* Through the base quaternion ⟨e_1,e_2,e_3⟩={1,2,3}, the three copies (3rd generator c∈{4,8,12}) have
ambient-L non-anticommuting-pair counts {0, 6, 12}.
These three properties are DISTINCT (8 ZD-free ⊋ 1 Clifford-pure); do not conflate them.

prove — Erratum E1's claim that Gresnigt's three family-S₃ octonion copies are non-monomial: only the
base octonion is Clifford-pure, so the ambient embedding already distinguishes it. The non-monomiality

contains S₃ subgroups, so a basis-index census cannot by itself separate the family-S₃ from an S₃
inside the monomial-168. Reported as an executed algebraic fingerprint, not a group-theoretic proof.
Uses e_i·e_j = σ(i,j)·e_{i⊕j}; {L_i,L_j}=0 via σ(i,j⊕c)σ(j,c)+σ(j,i⊕c)σ(i,c)=0 ∀c; a zero-divisor

comments: Finding 11 (issue #2084): u64 >>, /, % must use unsigned semantics.
At the dispatch point these three operations had a single BinaryOp variant
each (OpShr, OpDiv, OpRem) that the lowering always emitted as the signed
x86 instruction (sar rax,cl / idiv rcx). For a u64 value with bit 63 set
that gives mathematically wrong answers with no error:
- 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_u64 >> 1 expected 0x7FFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF (unsigned)
sar gives                    0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF (sign-extends)
- 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_u64 /  2 expected 0x7FFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF (unsigned)
idiv gives                            0 (treats as -1, truncate-toward-zero)
- 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_u64 %  2 expected                    1 (unsigned)
idiv gives                           -1 (i.e. the input unchanged)
Bit-63-set is the boundary: a value with bit 62 set already shifts correctly
because the sign bit stays 0 under sar. + - * & | ^ << == != are unaffected.
This fixture MUST fail on unfixed main (where the lowering always emits the
signed instruction) and PASS once BinaryOp carries OpUDiv/OpURem/OpUShr and
the lowering routes them to div r/m64 / shr rax,cl.
